stem:
A 29-year-old laboratory technician centrifuges a blood sample and observes three layers: a red layer at the bottom, a thin pale middle layer making up less than 1 percent of the volume, and straw-colored fluid on top.

Which of the following is the composition of the pale middle layer?

options.label: A
options.misconception: The densest cells are being placed in the middle layer.
options.explanation: Erythrocytes are the heaviest elements and settle at the very bottom of the tube; the pale middle buffy coat contains leukocytes and platelets.

options.label: B
options.misconception: The top fluid layer is being confused with the middle cellular layer.
options.explanation: Plasma — the straw-colored fluid with its proteins and solutes — forms the top layer above the buffy coat, not the pale middle band.

options.label: C
options.misconception: None; the buffy coat holds white cells and platelets.
options.explanation: Between the settled erythrocytes and the plasma sits the buffy coat, a pale thin layer of white blood cells (leukocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes) that normally constitutes less than 1 percent of a blood sample.

options.label: D
options.misconception: Soluble clotting proteins are being treated as a separate spun layer.
options.explanation: Clotting factors remain dissolved in the plasma layer above; the visible pale band between red cells and plasma is the cellular buffy coat.

options.label: E
options.misconception: Marrow-resident precursors are being imagined in peripheral blood.
options.explanation: Megakaryocytes remain in bone marrow; circulating blood's middle layer contains only leukocytes and the platelet fragments megakaryocytes release.

context: Learning objective: read a spun blood sample. Centrifugation separates blood by density: erythrocytes at the bottom (about 45 percent, the hematocrit), a thin buffy coat of leukocytes and platelets (under 1 percent) in the middle, and straw-colored plasma on top.
